```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Hosawi et al. fit maternal plasma and breast-milk hydroxyurea concentrations
from the Hydroxyurea Exposure in Lactation Study (HELPS, NCT02990598) and used
the model to estimate how much hydroxyurea a breastfed infant ingests at ages
0-9 months.

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Hosawi_2026_hydroxyurea"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Hosawi_2026_hydroxyurea"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.70394>

The structure (Figure 1 of the paper) is a two-compartment oral model with a
first-order absorption rate constant after a lag time, and a breast-milk
compartment that exchanges with the central compartment in both directions
through one clearance, `CL plasma-milk`. Drug is not eliminated from milk, so
over a single dose the area under the milk curve equals the area under the
plasma curve.

# Population

Sixteen lactating women each took a single oral 1000 mg dose of hydroxyurea
(about 15-20 mg/kg), giving 101 plasma and 93 breast-milk concentrations.
Plasma and milk were sampled before the dose and serially to 8-25 h after it;
two women gave milk samples only (Methods, "Patients and sampling"). The
paper does not tabulate demographics. A 1000 mg dose at 15-20 mg/kg implies
body weights of roughly 50-67 kg, which is the range used for the virtual
cohorts below. The same information is in the model's `population` metadata.

# Source trace

| Element | Value | Source location |
|---|---|---|
| Structure: depot, central, peripheral, breast milk | two-compartment, reversible milk compartment | Figure 1; Results, "Population PK modeling" |
| `lka` | 2.5 1/h | Table 1, `KA (/h)` |
| `ltlag` | 0.2 h | Table 1, `LAG Time (h)` |
| `lfdepot` | 1 (fixed) | Table 1, `F` = 1 Fixed |
| `lcl` | 8.57 L/h per 70 kg | Table 1, `CL (L/h/70 kg)` |
| `lvc` | 39.0 L per 70 kg | Table 1, `V(L/70 kg)` |
| `lq` | 4.4 L/h | Table 1, `Q (L/h)` |
| `lvp` | 19.1 L | Table 1, `V2 (L)` |
| `lq_milk` | 2.3 L/h | Table 1, `CL plasma-milk (L/h)` |
| `lvmilk` | 0.79 L | Table 1, `VM (L)` |
| `e_wt_cl`, `e_wt_vc` | 0.75, 1 (fixed), reference 70 kg | Methods, "Covariate analysis"; Table 1 units and footnote |
| `etalcl`, `etalvc`, `etalka`, `etaltlag`, `etalq_milk`, `etalvmilk` | 27.4, 42.3, 114, 43.7, 51.7, 23.2 CV% | Table 1, IIV rows; converted with Eq. 2, omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2) |
| `propSd` (plasma) | 0.15 | Table 1, `Prop.Err.(CV%)` = 15.0 |
| `addSd_Cmilk` (milk) | 1.12 ug/mL | Table 1, `Add.Err.` = 1.12 ug/mL |
| Infant milk intake, Eq. 3 | 160.39 x 0.232/(0.232 - 0.00252) x (exp(-0.00252 age) - exp(-0.232 age)) mL/kg/day, age in days | Methods, Eq. 3 (vignette only) |
| Infant daily dose, Eqs. 4-5 | sum over feeds of Cmilk x feed volume | Methods, Eqs. 4-5 (vignette only) |

# Single-dose profiles and the visual predictive check

The HELPS design is reproduced with 200 virtual women given 1000 mg, with body
weight drawn uniformly between 50 and 67 kg. Observation rows are on the
`central` state so both `Cc` and `Cmilk` come back at every time.

```{r helps-sim}
mod <- readModelDb("Hosawi_2026_hydroxyurea")

n_women <- 200
set.seed(20261025)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261025)
cohort <- tibble(id = seq_len(n_women), WT = runif(n_women, 50, 67))

grid <- sort(unique(c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, seq(1, 12, by = 0.5), seq(13, 48, by = 1))))
ev_helps <- bind_rows(
  cohort |> mutate(time = 0, amt = 1000, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", dvid = NA_integer_),
  tidyr::expand_grid(cohort, time = grid) |>
    mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", dvid = 1L)
) |>
  mutate(treatment = "1000 mg single dose") |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))

sim_helps <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod, ev_helps,
  returnType = "data.frame", keep = c("WT", "treatment")
)
```

Figure 4 of the paper is a VPC of the observed data. The points below are the
observed medians read off Figure 4 by the maintainers (approximate, to the
nearest 0.5 ug/mL), drawn over the simulated 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles
of the model prediction without residual error.

```{r vpc, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
obs_median <- tibble::tribble(
  ~matrix, ~time, ~conc,
  "Maternal plasma", 0.5, 4.5,
  "Maternal plasma", 1, 18,
  "Maternal plasma", 2, 16.5,
  "Maternal plasma", 3, 12,
  "Maternal plasma", 4, 10,
  "Maternal plasma", 6, 7,
  "Maternal plasma", 8, 4.5,
  "Breast milk", 1, 3.5,
  "Breast milk", 2, 13.5,
  "Breast milk", 3, 11,
  "Breast milk", 4, 8,
  "Breast milk", 6, 5.5,
  "Breast milk", 8, 4,
  "Breast milk", 11, 2.5
)

vpc <- sim_helps |>
  filter(time <= 14) |>
  select(id, time, `Maternal plasma` = Cc, `Breast milk` = Cmilk) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(id, time), names_to = "matrix", values_to = "conc") |>
  group_by(matrix, time) |>
  summarise(
    p10 = quantile(conc, 0.1), p50 = median(conc), p90 = quantile(conc, 0.9),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(vpc, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p10, ymax = p90), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(aes(y = p50)) +
  geom_point(data = obs_median, aes(y = conc), colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(matrix, c("Maternal plasma", "Breast milk")), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "Hydroxyurea (ug/mL)",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 4 of Hosawi 2026. Red points: observed medians read off Figure 4."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r vpc-table}
vpc_cmp <- obs_median |>
  inner_join(vpc |> select(matrix, time, p50), by = c("matrix", "time")) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = round(100 * (p50 / conc - 1)))
vpc_cmp |>
  rename(
    Matrix = matrix, `Time (h)` = time, `Observed median (Fig. 4)` = conc,
    `Simulated median` = p50, `Difference (%)` = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

From 1 h onward the simulated plasma medians fall within the scatter of the
observed medians in Figure 4. The largest plasma differences are at 0.5 h, on
the steep rising limb, where the lag time and the 114% CV on KA make the
median very sensitive to the exact sampling time. Milk is different: from
2 h onward the simulated milk median runs 30-40% above the observed medians
(plasma: within about 10%), and above the model-predicted median band that the
paper draws in Figure 4, which sits at roughly 0.8-0.85 times plasma. The printed structure cannot put
milk below plasma (see "Milk concentrations run above the paper's" under
Assumptions and deviations).

# PKNCA: clearance and the milk-plasma mass balance

The paper reports no NCA. Two checks follow from the model structure itself:
the apparent clearance from NCA, dose / AUC0-inf of plasma, must equal each
woman's own `cl`; and because milk has no elimination, milk AUC0-inf must
equal plasma AUC0-inf. Both are compared within each woman, on the same
drawn parameters, so the remaining difference is only extrapolation and
trapezoidal error.

```{r pknca}
conc_nca <- sim_helps |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  select(id, time, treatment, `Maternal plasma` = Cc, `Breast milk` = Cmilk) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Maternal plasma`, `Breast milk`), names_to = "matrix", values_to = "conc")
dose_nca <- ev_helps |>
  filter(evid == 1) |>
  select(id, time, amt, treatment)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_nca, conc ~ time | treatment + matrix + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_nca, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = Inf,
  cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, half.life = TRUE, cl.obs = TRUE
)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
nca <- as.data.frame(nca_res)

nca |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "tmax", "aucinf.obs", "half.life")) |>
  group_by(matrix, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(
    median = signif(median(PPORRES, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    p5 = signif(quantile(PPORRES, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    p95 = signif(quantile(PPORRES, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(Matrix = matrix, `NCA parameter` = PPTESTCD, Median = median, `5th pct` = p5, `95th pct` = p95) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Simulated NCA after a single 1000 mg dose (200 women, 50-67 kg).")
```

```{r pknca-checks}
indiv_cl <- sim_helps |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(cl_model = first(cl), .groups = "drop")

cl_chk <- nca |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "cl.obs", matrix == "Maternal plasma") |>
  select(id, cl_nca = PPORRES) |>
  inner_join(indiv_cl, by = "id") |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (cl_nca / cl_model - 1))

auc_chk <- nca |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "aucinf.obs") |>
  select(id, matrix, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = matrix, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (`Breast milk` / `Maternal plasma` - 1))

summary(cl_chk$pct_diff)
summary(auc_chk$pct_diff)

stopifnot(
  # NCA CL/F against each woman's own model clearance: extrapolation and
  # trapezoidal error only.
  abs(median(cl_chk$pct_diff)) < 3,
  # Milk and plasma AUC0-inf agree within a woman (mass balance; milk has no
  # elimination route). The milk curve lags plasma, so the extrapolated tail
  # carries slightly more of the milk AUC.
  abs(median(auc_chk$pct_diff)) < 3
)
```

For the typical 70 kg woman, NCA clearance reproduces the paper's estimate of
8.57 L/h (Table 1 and Discussion):

```{r pknca-typical}
ev_typ <- bind_rows(
  tibble(id = 1L, time = 0, amt = 1000, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", dvid = NA_integer_),
  tibble(id = 1L, time = grid, amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", dvid = 1L)
) |>
  mutate(WT = 70, treatment = "1000 mg, typical 70 kg")
# A one-subject solve returns no id column; add it back for PKNCA.
typ <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev_typ, omega = NA, sigma = NA, returnType = "data.frame", keep = "treatment") |>
  mutate(id = 1L)

typ_nca <- as.data.frame(PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(typ |> filter(!is.na(Cc)), Cc ~ time | treatment + id),
  PKNCA::PKNCAdose(ev_typ |> filter(evid == 1), amt ~ time | treatment + id),
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, aucinf.obs = TRUE, cl.obs = TRUE)
)))

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = typ_nca |> filter(PPTESTCD == "cl.obs"),
  reference = tibble(treatment = "1000 mg, typical 70 kg", cl.obs = 8.57),
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(cl.obs = "L/h"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = "Typical-subject NCA clearance vs the Table 1 CL estimate.")
stopifnot(abs(typ_nca$PPORRES[typ_nca$PPTESTCD == "cl.obs"] / 8.57 - 1) < 0.02)
```

# Infant exposure through breastfeeding (Table 2 and Figure 5)

The paper simulated 1000 women given 20 mg/kg at time zero and predicted milk
concentrations over the following 24 h. Infant daily milk intake comes from
the weight-normalised intake curve (Eq. 3, age in days); each feed volume is
the daily intake divided by the number of feeds per day, the dose per feed is
the milk concentration at the feed time times the feed volume (Eq. 4), and
the infant's daily dose is the sum over feeds (Eq. 5).

Eq. 3 is checked against the peak the paper reports, 152.6 mL/kg/day at 19.7
days:

```{r milk-intake}
milk_intake <- function(age_days) {
  160.39 * 0.232 / (0.232 - 0.00252) *
    (exp(-0.00252 * age_days) - exp(-0.232 * age_days))
}
peak_age <- log(0.232 / 0.00252) / (0.232 - 0.00252)
c(peak_age_days = peak_age, peak_intake = milk_intake(peak_age))
stopifnot(
  abs(peak_age - 19.7) < 0.05,
  abs(milk_intake(peak_age) - 152.6) < 0.05
)
```

Feeding frequency follows the paper's age groups as tabulated in Table 2: 12
feeds/day up to 30 days, 9 up to 60 days, 8 up to 90 days, 6 up to 180 days
and 4 thereafter. The paper does not state the clock times of the feeds;
they are taken here as evenly spaced, the first one dosing interval after the
maternal dose (at 24/n, 2 x 24/n, ..., 24 h).

```{r infant-sim}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261026)
cohort20 <- tibble(id = seq_len(n_women), WT = runif(n_women, 50, 67))
# Every feed time of every feeding frequency is put on the grid (24/9 h is
# not a multiple of 0.25 h); rounding makes the later matching exact.
feed_grid <- unlist(lapply(c(12, 9, 8, 6, 4), function(n) seq_len(n) * 24 / n))
grid24 <- sort(unique(round(c(seq(0, 24, by = 0.25), feed_grid), 6)))
ev20 <- bind_rows(
  cohort20 |> mutate(time = 0, amt = 20 * WT, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", dvid = NA_integer_),
  tidyr::expand_grid(cohort20, time = grid24) |>
    mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", dvid = 1L)
) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
sim20 <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev20, returnType = "data.frame", keep = "WT") |>
  select(id, time, Cmilk)

# Upper bounds inclusive, as Table 2 assigns 12 feeds to month 1 and 9 to
# month 2; Figure 5 steps down just after 60, 90 and 180 days.
feeds_per_day <- function(age_days) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    age_days <= 30 ~ 12L,
    age_days <= 60 ~ 9L,
    age_days <= 90 ~ 8L,
    age_days <= 180 ~ 6L,
    TRUE ~ 4L
  )
}

infant_dose <- function(age_days, intake = milk_intake(age_days)) {
  n_feed <- feeds_per_day(age_days)
  feed_times <- round(seq_len(n_feed) * 24 / n_feed, 6)
  fed <- sim20 |>
    filter(round(time, 6) %in% feed_times)
  stopifnot(nrow(fed) == n_feed * n_women)
  fed |>
    group_by(id) |>
    # Cmilk ug/mL x feed volume mL/kg = ug/kg per feed; /1000 -> mg/kg.
    summarise(dose_mgkg = sum(Cmilk * intake / n_feed) / 1000, .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(age_days = age_days, n_feed = n_feed, intake = intake)
}
```

Table 2 lists its milk intakes per month; those values are used directly so
that the comparison isolates the pharmacokinetic part of the calculation.

```{r table2}
table2 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~month, ~intake, ~feeds, ~median, ~p5, ~p95,
  1, 150.3, 12, 0.75, 0.44, 1.30,
  2, 139.6, 9, 0.71, 0.41, 1.23,
  3, 129.5, 8, 0.59, 0.34, 1.03,
  4, 120.1, 6, 0.49, 0.28, 0.87,
  5, 111.4, 6, 0.46, 0.26, 0.80,
  6, 103.4, 6, 0.43, 0.24, 0.75,
  7, 95.9, 4, 0.32, 0.18, 0.56,
  8, 89.0, 4, 0.30, 0.17, 0.52,
  9, 82.6, 4, 0.27, 0.16, 0.48
)

sim_t2 <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(table2)), function(i) {
  infant_dose(table2$month[i] * 30, intake = table2$intake[i]) |>
    mutate(month = table2$month[i])
})) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(
    n_feed = first(n_feed),
    sim_median = median(dose_mgkg),
    sim_p5 = quantile(dose_mgkg, 0.05),
    sim_p95 = quantile(dose_mgkg, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  inner_join(table2, by = "month") |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (sim_median / median - 1))

stopifnot(all(sim_t2$n_feed == sim_t2$feeds))

sim_t2 |>
  transmute(
    month, intake, feeds,
    published = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, p5, p95),
    simulated = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", sim_median, sim_p5, sim_p95),
    pct_diff = round(pct_diff)
  ) |>
  rename(
    `Age (months)` = month, `Milk intake (mL/kg/day)` = intake,
    `Feeds/day` = feeds, `Table 2 median (5th-95th)` = published,
    `Simulated median (5th-95th)` = simulated, `Median difference (%)` = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Infant daily hydroxyurea dose (mg/kg/day): simulated vs Table 2.")

stopifnot(
  # Centre: a mis-transcribed CL, V or milk parameter, or a ug/mL vs mg/L
  # slip, moves every month by far more than this.
  abs(median(sim_t2$pct_diff)) < 30,
  # The paper's conclusion: every age stays below the 10% RID threshold of
  # 2 mg/kg/day, including the upper 95th percentile.
  all(sim_t2$sim_p95 < 2)
)
```

The simulated medians run about 10-25% above Table 2 in every month. The
month-to-month pattern matches closely, including the drop each time the
number of feeds per day falls: with fewer, more widely spaced feeds, the feed
times miss more of the milk concentration peak. The constant offset is the
same milk over-prediction seen in the VPC above; it comes from the printed
model structure, not from the virtual cohort (see "Milk concentrations run
above the paper's" under Assumptions and deviations). Every month stays well
below the 2 mg/kg/day threshold, so the paper's conclusion is unchanged.

```{r fig5, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
ages <- c(0, 2, 4, 7, seq(10, 40, by = 5), seq(50, 270, by = 10))
fig5 <- bind_rows(lapply(ages, infant_dose))

ggplot(fig5, aes(factor(age_days), dose_mgkg)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "steelblue", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = as.character(seq(0, 260, by = 20))) +
  labs(
    x = "Infant age (days)", y = "Infant daily dose (mg/kg/day)",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 5 of Hosawi 2026. Blue line: 10% RID threshold (2 mg/kg/day)."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Milk concentrations run above the paper's.** The model is transcribed
  exactly as printed: Figure 1 draws one bidirectional plasma-milk clearance
  between central and the milk compartment, with elimination from central
  only, and Table 1 gives that clearance (2.3 L/h) and the milk volume
  (0.79 L) but no milk:plasma partition coefficient, no second (asymmetric)
  transfer clearance and no loss from milk. With symmetric exchange and no
  loss, milk AUC0-inf must equal plasma AUC0-inf (the PKNCA check above
  confirms it) and milk sits at or above plasma after its peak. The paper's
  own outputs imply milk at about 0.8-0.85 times plasma: the model-predicted
  milk median in Figure 4 is about 11, 9.6, 7.9 and 5.4 ug/mL at 2, 3, 4 and
  6 h (read off the figure), while this model gives about 17.0, 13.7, 10.6
  and 6.9 ug/mL for a typical 70 kg woman; and the Table 2 infant doses imply
  a mean milk concentration about 15-20% below this model's. The authors'
  NONMEM implementation therefore probably contains a term that the paper
  does not report. No such term was added here, because its value would have
  to be tuned to the figures rather than taken from the paper. Plasma is
  unaffected. Infant doses from this model are 10-25% higher than Table 2,
  and the paper's conclusion (every age below the 10% relative infant dose
  threshold of 2 mg/kg/day) holds either way.
* **Allometric scaling applies to CL and V only.** The Methods say body
  weight was evaluated with theoretical exponents on CL and Q (0.75) and on V
  and V2 (1). Table 1, however, reports CL and V per 70 kg and Q, V2, the
  plasma-milk clearance and VM in plain L/h and L, and its footnote names
  only CL and V as size-standardised; the Discussion likewise says body
  weight influenced "clearance and volume of distribution". The model follows
  Table 1 and scales CL and V only. For women near 70 kg the choice makes
  little difference.
* **Residual error values are standard deviations.** The Methods state that
  CV% values for omega^2 and sigma^2 were computed from the square roots of
  the variances, so the proportional 15.0% is taken as an SD of 0.15 and the
  additive 1.12 ug/mL as an SD.
* **IIV conversion.** Table 1 IIV values are CV%; Eq. 2 is the log-normal
  formula, so omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2).
* **Body weight of the cohorts.** The paper does not tabulate HELPS
  demographics, and its infant-exposure simulation used NHANES-based women
  with weights "consistent with the HELPS study population" without giving
  the distribution. Both virtual cohorts here draw weight uniformly from 50
  to 67 kg, the range implied by a 1000 mg dose at about 15-20 mg/kg. The
  cohorts have 200 women, not the paper's 1000.
* **Feed timing.** The paper does not give feed clock times. Feeds are
  evenly spaced, the first one dosing interval (24/n h) after the maternal
  dose. Starting the feeds at the time of the dose instead lowers each
  infant dose by a few percent and does not change the conclusions.
* **Ages in Table 2.** Month k is evaluated at 30k days. The Table 2 milk
  intakes themselves are used for the comparison, because Eq. 3 at 30k days
  gives values up to 0.5 mL/kg/day lower than Table 2 (for example 150.2
  versus 150.3 at 1 month and 129.2 versus 129.5 at 3 months).
* **Feeding-frequency age bands.** The Methods define the groups as 0 to <1
  month (12/day), 1 to <2 months (9), 2-3 months (8), 4-6 months (6) and 7-9
  months (4-5), but Table 2 gives 12 feeds at 1 month and 9 at 2 months, and
  Figure 5 steps down just after 60, 90 and 180 days. The vignette follows
  Table 2 and Figure 5: 12 feeds up to 30 days, 9 up to 60, 8 up to 90, 6 up
  to 180 and 4 thereafter (Table 2 uses 4, not 5, for 7-9 months).
* **Clinical status of the HELPS women.** The paper does not say whether the
  women had sickle cell anaemia, so the model's `population` metadata leaves
  it unstated.
